findings.title: Hung flusher processes are no longer killed before a replacement is spawned
findings.body:
The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is true. Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so the check is always False in production.

When a process is flagged as a `hang`, the still-alive old process is left running and a second process is started for the same shards. Both share the same `stopped`, `current_drift`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values. Consequences:
- Two processes can call `flush_segments` on the same shards concurrently and produce duplicate segments to buffered-segments.
- The stale process can keep refreshing `healthy_since`, masking the new one's health.
- Up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS orphan processes can leak.

The same broken check at line 346 means `terminate()` in `join()` never runs either. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for not being a `threading.Thread`) instead.

findings.title: join() breaks out of the loop on deadline and skips terminating the remaining processes
findings.body:
In `join()`, once the deadline has passed, `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the loop entirely. Every process after that point never reaches the `process.terminate()` call. Before this change, terminate was always attempted after the wait.

With several flusher processes, a timed-out join (e.g. during rebalancing) leaves the later processes running unsupervised. They can keep flushing shards that may now belong to another consumer. A stuck process would never exit, because it is only stopped via the `stopped` flag.

The deadline check should only skip the waiting, not the termination.

findings.title: Cluster-wide Redis memory info is queried once per flusher buffer on every submit
findings.body:
`get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not for a shard. The new loop calls it once per per-process buffer, so every `submit()` issues N times as many INFO calls to every cluster node.

The used/available ratio comes out the same only because both sums are multiplied by N. The extra calls are pure overhead on the consumer's main thread, which this PR is trying to keep minimal.

`record_stored_segments` is likewise split into N separate pipelines. Query memory info once (e.g. from a single buffer) instead.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}`. `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards that group or filter these flusher metrics by one key will silently miss the other metric.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.
